passages.title: Life without rain: how desert plants survive
paras: Deserts are usually defined as places that receive less than 250 millimetres of rain a year, but the total amount of rain is only part of the challenge for the plants that live there. Rain in deserts is also unpredictable: a year’s worth may fall in a single afternoon, followed by many months of complete drought. Temperatures can rise above 45 degrees Celsius during the day and fall close to freezing at night. Despite these conditions, deserts support a surprising variety of plant life, and botanists have identified three broad strategies that allow plants to survive.

The first strategy is simply to avoid the drought altogether. Many desert plants are annuals, which means they complete their entire life cycle within a single season. Their seeds can lie in the soil for years, sometimes decades, waiting for enough rain. When a heavy shower finally arrives, they germinate within days, grow quickly, flower and produce new seeds before the ground dries out again. For a few weeks the desert may be covered in flowers, an event that attracts tourists to some regions. Interestingly, the seeds of many species contain chemicals that stop them from germinating after a light shower. Only a substantial amount of rain washes these chemicals away, which prevents the seeds from sprouting when there is not enough water for the plant to complete its life cycle.

The second strategy is to store water. The best-known example is the cactus, which is native to the Americas, although similar plants, known as succulents, are found in deserts all over the world. These plants have thick, fleshy stems or leaves in which large quantities of water can be kept. A large cactus can hold several hundred litres after a storm. Many cacti have pleated stems which expand like an accordion as they fill with water and shrink again as the water is used up. Their spines, which are in fact highly modified leaves, protect this valuable store from thirsty animals, and also provide a little shade for the surface of the stem.

Storing water is only useful, however, if the plant can avoid losing it. All plants lose water through tiny pores, called stomata, which they must open to take in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis. Most plants open their stomata during the day, when photosynthesis takes place, but this is also when the air is hottest and driest. Many succulents have developed a different system. They open their stomata only at night, when it is cooler, and store the carbon dioxide in the form of an acid. During the day, with the stomata firmly closed, they use this stored carbon dioxide to photosynthesise. This system is slower than normal photosynthesis, which partly explains why cacti grow so slowly, but it can reduce water loss by as much as 90 per cent.

The third strategy involves the plant’s roots. Some desert shrubs and trees send their roots extraordinarily deep in search of underground water. The roots of one species of acacia have been found more than 30 metres below the surface. Other plants take the opposite approach and spread a dense network of shallow roots just below the surface over a wide area. These roots can absorb water from even a light shower before it evaporates. A few species have both kinds, so they can benefit from rain on the surface while also reaching permanent water further down.

Leaves present a particular problem in the desert, as they provide a large surface through which water can escape. Many desert plants therefore have very small leaves, or lose their leaves entirely during the driest months. Others have leaves covered in fine hairs, which reflect sunlight and trap a thin layer of moist air close to the surface. Some have a waxy coating that acts like a waterproof layer. The colour of desert plants also tends to be pale grey or silver rather than dark green, which reduces the amount of heat they absorb.

Scientists are increasingly interested in desert plants, and not only for their own sake. As the climate changes and many farming regions become hotter and drier, researchers hope that genes from desert species might one day be used to develop food crops that need less water. Progress so far has been modest, because the features that help desert plants survive often come at the cost of slow growth, which is exactly what farmers do not want. Nevertheless, understanding how these remarkable plants manage with so little water may prove valuable in a world where fresh water is becoming an increasingly precious resource.

passages.title: Farming upwards: the rise of the vertical farm
paras: In a former warehouse on the edge of a large city, rows of lettuces grow under purple light, stacked in towers that reach almost to the ceiling. There is no soil, no sunlight and no weather. Computers control the temperature, the humidity and the nutrients that flow past the plants’ roots. This is a vertical farm, and supporters claim that farms like it could transform the way cities are fed. Critics, however, argue that the idea has been oversold, and that vertical farming will remain a small and expensive niche.

The basic idea is not new. Growing plants without soil, a technique known as hydroponics, has been used in greenhouses for decades. What is new is the scale and the level of control. Instead of a single layer of crops, vertical farms grow plants on many levels, sometimes ten or more. Because the space is completely enclosed, growers can adjust every condition to suit the crop. Some farms even change the colour of their lights at different stages of growth, since plants respond to particular wavelengths.

The advantages are considerable. A vertical farm can produce many times more food per square metre of land than a conventional field, because it uses height as well as area and because crops can be harvested all year round. Water use is dramatically lower, as the water is recycled rather than lost to the soil or evaporation; some operators claim savings of more than 90 per cent. Since there are no insects in a sealed building, pesticides are unnecessary. And because the farms can be built in cities, close to the people who eat the food, vegetables can reach shops within hours of being picked, rather than days.

The main problem is energy. In a field, sunlight is free; in a vertical farm, every photon has to be produced by an electric light. Lighting is usually the largest single cost, followed by the air-conditioning needed to remove the heat that the lights produce. As a result, the environmental benefits depend heavily on where the electricity comes from. A farm powered by coal may produce lettuce with a larger carbon footprint than lettuce grown in a field and transported hundreds of kilometres by lorry.

Cost also limits which crops make sense. At present, vertical farms grow mainly leafy greens and herbs such as lettuce, spinach and basil. These plants grow quickly, are small and are almost entirely edible, so very little of the expensive light is wasted on parts that cannot be sold. Staple crops such as wheat and rice, by contrast, take months to mature and are sold at very low prices. One researcher calculated that wheat grown in a vertical farm would cost several times more than imported wheat, even under ideal conditions.

Several high-profile vertical farming companies have closed in recent years, which has led some observers to declare the whole industry a failure. Yet others see these closures as a normal part of a young industry’s development. The cost of LED lighting has fallen sharply over the past decade, and the lights have become far more efficient. Some newer farms are being built next to sources of cheap renewable energy, or in places where waste heat from factories can be reused.

The technology may also prove especially valuable in places where conventional farming is difficult. In hot, dry countries that import most of their fresh vegetables, vertical farms offer a way to grow produce locally with very little water. Similar arguments apply to cold northern regions with short growing seasons, and to remote communities where fresh food must be flown in at great expense. In such places, the comparison is not with cheap field-grown crops, but with expensive imports.

It seems unlikely, then, that vertical farms will replace traditional agriculture. They will not feed the world with bread or rice. But as part of a wider food system, supplying fresh, local vegetables to cities and to regions with harsh climates, they may yet find a lasting and useful place.

passages.title: In praise of boredom?
passages.subtitle: Psychologists are divided over whether being bored is bad for us or a hidden source of creativity.
paras: Few experiences are as universally disliked as boredom. We fill every empty moment, at bus stops, in queues, even at traffic lights, by reaching for our phones. Parents rush to entertain children who complain that they have nothing to do, and employers worry about staff who find their work dull. Yet a growing number of psychologists have begun to ask whether boredom deserves its bad reputation. Perhaps, they suggest, the uncomfortable feeling of having nothing to do serves a purpose, and in eliminating it we may be losing something valuable.

Part of the difficulty is that boredom has proved surprisingly hard to define. Early researchers treated it simply as a lack of stimulation: the state of a person in a dull environment. More recent work has emphasised attention instead. In this view, boredom is the feeling we have when we want to be engaged in something satisfying but are unable to be, either because nothing around us interests us or because we cannot concentrate on what is in front of us. The psychologist Maren Lindqvist describes it as “an itch for meaning that cannot be scratched”. This explains why people can feel bored even when surrounded by things to do.

The case for boredom rests largely on its connection with creativity. In one frequently cited experiment, a team led by Dr Paul Ferrante asked one group of volunteers to spend fifteen minutes copying numbers from a telephone directory, a deliberately tedious task, while a second group went straight to the next stage. Both groups were then asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. Those who had been bored first came up with significantly more ideas. Ferrante concluded that boredom pushes the mind to wander, and that a wandering mind is more likely to make unusual connections.

Not everyone is convinced. Critics point out that experiments like Ferrante’s involve short periods of mild boredom in a laboratory, which may have little in common with the chronic boredom that some people experience at work or at school. The sociologist Hannah Okafor argues that it is misleading to generalise from a quarter of an hour of copying numbers to the experience of a factory worker repeating the same task for years. Moreover, attempts by other researchers to repeat Ferrante’s results have produced mixed findings, with some studies finding a creative benefit and others finding none.

There is also substantial evidence that boredom can be harmful. People who report being bored frequently are more likely to eat unhealthily, to take risks and to perform poorly at school. Boredom at work has been linked to mistakes and accidents. Some researchers believe the direction of cause and effect is unclear: it may be that people who are already unhappy are more likely to describe themselves as bored, rather than boredom causing their unhappiness. Even so, the association is consistent enough to make most psychologists cautious about recommending boredom as a remedy for anything.

A more balanced position is taken by Dr Samuel Ito, who distinguishes between the feeling of boredom and what we do in response to it. Boredom, he suggests, is best understood as a signal, rather like hunger or pain, telling us that our current activity is not meeting our needs. Like those signals, it is neither good nor bad in itself. What matters is how we respond. If we respond by reflecting on our goals or by seeking a more meaningful activity, boredom can lead to positive change. If we respond by seeking any distraction available, the signal is silenced but the underlying problem remains.

It is this second response, Ito believes, that modern technology has made almost automatic. Smartphones offer an endless supply of easy distraction, so that the feeling of boredom rarely lasts long enough to prompt any reflection. In his view, the danger is not that we are bored too often, but that we are no longer bored for long enough for the feeling to do its job. This is an attractive argument, though it should be said that there is as yet little direct evidence for it.

What, then, should we do? The answer is probably not to seek out boredom deliberately, nor to fill every moment in an effort to avoid it. Instead, we might simply tolerate the feeling a little longer before reaching for a distraction, and ask what it is telling us. For children, this may mean allowing them to find their own ways to occupy themselves rather than organising every hour. The occasional empty afternoon, it seems, may be less of a problem than we think.
